summaries.summary: NMT relies on large-scale parallel data, performs poorly on low-resource or zero-resource pairs, and pivot-based methods double decoding time and propagate translation errors.
Transfer learning initializes a low-resource source→target child model from a high-resource pivot→target parent model but performs very poorly without child training data.
The language space mismatch problem, also named domain shift problem, causes zero-shot transfer failure because source and pivot feature distributions are not explicitly aligned.
The paper studies zero-shot transfer with source↔pivot and pivot↔target data but no source↔target data, proposing cross-lingual pre-training and BRidge Language Modeling (BRLM).
The paper proposes a new transfer learning approach for NMT using cross-lingual language model pre-training to enable high performance on zero-shot translation.
The paper proposes a novel pre-training method called BRLM that effectively alleviates the distance between different source language spaces.

The proposed approach significantly improves zero-shot translation performance, consistently surpassing pivoting and multilingual approaches while maintaining or improving supervised translation direction performance.
Zero-shot translation in NMT has attracted widespread attention, with existing methods divided into pivot-based method, transfer learning, multilingual NMT, and unsupervised NMT.
Pivot-based Method includes pivoting and pivot-synthetic, but faces quadratic growth in source languages, computation expense, parameter vastness, and error propagation.
Transfer Learning for NMT uses a high-resource parent model to initialize a low-resource child model, with shared vocabularies or cross-lingual word embedding, but has limited zero-shot effects.

Multilingual NMT (MNMT) supports multiple source and target languages and unseen pairs, but zero-shot translation easily fails, is sensitive to hyper-parameter setting, and often underperforms pivoting.
Unsupervised NMT (UNMT) uses only large-scale monolingual corpora and performs well between similar languages, but distant-language performance remains far from expectation.
The proposed method belongs to transfer learning but uses cross-lingual pre-training before parent model training to make all source languages share the same feature space.
The section presents a cross-lingual pre-training based transfer approach for zero-shot scenarios with source↔pivot and pivot↔target bilingual data but no source↔target parallel data.
The first step pre-trains a universal encoder with source/pivot monolingual or source↔pivot bilingual data.
The second step trains a pivot→target parent model on the pre-trained universal encoder with available parallel data while freezing several layers to avoid degeneracy.
The third step directly translates source sentences into target sentences with the parent model, benefiting from the universal encoder.
The key difficulty is ensuring language-invariant intermediate representations, and the section presents two existing methods, a new cross-lingual pre-training method, and the transfer protocol.
Masked Language Modeling (MLM) and Translation Language Modeling (TLM) are effective on XNLI cross-lingual classification but understudied for zero-shot cross-lingual generation tasks.
MLM adopts the Cloze objective of BERT, predicts randomly masked words replaced with [MASK] token on monolingual corpora, and maps shared word pieces into a shared space.
TLM extends MLM by concatenating sentence pairs, masking words in both source and target sentences, and resetting target sentence positions to count from zero.
BRidge Language Modeling (BRLM) is proposed to obtain word-level representation alignment by inferring masked words from aligned words on the other language side.
BRLM stacks a shared encoder over both side sentences separately and includes Hard Alignment (BRLM-HA) and Soft Alignment (BRLM-SA) structures.
Hard Alignment (BRLM-HA) uses an external aligner tool on source↔pivot parallel data and predicts masked words from surrounding words and aligned encoder outputs.
Soft Alignment (BRLM-SA) uses an additional attention layer to learn alignment information, avoid wrong external alignments, and enable many-to-one soft alignment.
MLM and TLM learn implicit alignment inefficiently or lack explicit source-target alignment, while BRLM uses alignment information for better word-level representation alignment.
The typical zero-shot translation scenario has a high resource pivot language parallel with source and target languages, and the approach has pretraining and transfer phases.
The pretraining phase pretrains MLM on source and pivot monolingual corpora, then continues TLM or BRLM on source-pivot parallel data to build a shared cross-lingual encoder.
The transfer phase trains a pivot→target NMT model initialized by the cross-lingually pre-trained encoder, freezes several layers, and transfers it to source→target translation.
For scenarios with multiple languages on the source or target side, the encoder and decoder are shared across each side languages for efficient deployment.
The approach is evaluated against strong baselines on Europarl and MultiUN, which contain multi-parallel evaluation data, using BLEU as the automatic metric.

Europarl evaluates Fr-En-Es, De-En-Fr and Ro-En-De with English as pivot, using devtest2006, test2006, 1,000 overlapping newstest2016 sentences, 2,000 validation sentences, and 60K BPE sub-word tokens.
MultiUN uses English (En) as pivot with Arabic (Ar), Spanish (Es), and Russian (Ru), six zero-shot directions, 80K BPE splits, tokenize.perl tokenization, and lowercased data.

Baselines are traditional transfer learning, pivot-based method and multilingual NMT, with Transformer-big, 1024 embedding/hidden units, 4096 feed-forward filter size, 6 layers, 8 heads, batch size 2400, 100 BPE tokens, attn_drop=0, XLM initialization, Adam with lr=0.0001, t_warm_up=4000, dropout=0.1, and length penalty α=1.0.

MLM+TLM and MLM+BRLM initialize TLM and BRLM from MLM, mask 15% of BPE tokens with 80% [MASK], 10% random BPE token, 10% unchanged, use masked-word prediction accuracy for stopping, and use fastalign for BRLM-HA.
Table TABREF19 and TABREF26 show the approaches consistently outperform pivoting, multilingual NMT (MNMT), and cross-lingual transfer without pretraining across languages and datasets.
On Europarl, pivoting is the strongest baseline, while cross-lingual transfer for languages without shared vocabularies performs worst because it does not use source↔pivot parallel data.
MLM+BRLM-SA achieves superior zero-shot performance on Europarl, improving by 0.9-4.8 BLEU points over pivoting and outperforming the original supervised Transformer in pivot→target.
MLM alone outperforms cross-lingual transfer and is comparable to pivoting, while MLM+BRLM-SA performs best and shows soft alignment is more helpful than hard alignment.
On MultiUN, MLM+BRLM-SA performs best among proposed cross-lingual pretraining transfer approaches and significantly outperforms MNMT BIBREF19 for one encoder-decoder model zero-shot translation.
MLM+BRLM-SA exceeds strong pivoting_m on Es → Ar and Es → Ru, and with back translation surpasses pivoting_m by 2.4 BLEU points averagely and MNMT BIBREF22 by 4.6 BLEU points averagely.

Using max-pooling and cosine similarity on Europarl validation sets, MLM+BRLM-SA shows the most stable similar cross-lingual sentence representations on all layers and best zero-shot translation performance.
Visualizing an English-Russian MultiUN validation sentence pair, MLM+BRLM-SA hidden states show higher similarity for two aligned words, indicating better word-level representation alignment.
On MultiUN test set with MLM+BRLM-SA, freezing the first four transformer layers performs best, balancing pre-training and fine-tuning between zero-shot and supervised directions.
The paper proposes a cross-lingual pretraining based transfer approach for zero-shot translation, introducing one monolingual and two bilingual pretraining methods to build a universal encoder.
The authors thank anonymous reviewers and acknowledge support from National Key R&D Program of China, National Natural Science Foundation of China, Alibaba Group, and PAPD.
